Together, these advances open the door to tracking not only ultrafast structural changes in solution, but also the evolving solvent environments that govern molecular behaviour and reactivity.

title: Tunable Near-Unity Light Absorption via Surface Exciton-Polaritons in Periodic Gratings of Anisotropic Polarizable Materials
abstract: Near-perfect light absorption in ultrathin films is hindered by two fundamental obstacles: the momentum mismatch that prevents resonant excitation of surface exciton-polaritons (SEPs) under ordinary illumination, and the 50% absorption ceiling imposed on free-standing conductive sheets by geometric symmetry. Here we show that both obstacles can be overcome simultaneously in a simple, planar geometry. A one-dimensional periodic grating of anisotropic polarizable ribbons composed of J-aggregates supporting bright molecular excitons provides the reciprocal lattice momentum needed to excite SEPs without employing an attenuated total reflection configuration, while a metallic mirror beneath a dielectric spacer folds the reflected field back onto the absorber, breaking the $50\%$ limit through interference between the incident and reflected waves. We develop a semi-analytical matrix formulation to compute the full optical response of such structure, and demonstrate that the absorptance at the first-order SEP resonance can be continuously tuned from near-unity to near-zero by varying the spacer thickness alone. The grating period and filling factor offer additional spectral control, and oblique incidence unlocks a second, out-of-plane polariton branch. These results establish periodic gratings of excitonic media as a versatile, practical and integrable platform for spectrally selective, near-perfect light absorption.

title: Designed atomic displacements for finite-temperature phonons from few force calculations
abstract: Finite-temperature phonons are usually fitted to first-principles forces in randomly displaced supercells, and each force calculation can be expensive. We introduce special optimal thermal cells (SOTCs), in which the displacements are designed rather than drawn at random. Our design, SOTC-D, starts from a harmonic trial model. It gives every supercell phonon mode its quantum-thermal amplitude, chooses the sign of each mode so that the force constants are best determined, and pairs each configuration with its inverse so that cubic forces cancel. Updating the trial leads to the self-consistent harmonic solution. Cells that match displacement correlations instead give good thermodynamics but not better dispersions. For eleven crystals, eight force calculations reproduce the effective dispersions within 0.03-0.31 THz, and SOTC-D is the most accurate of five designs in 9 of them. After one trial update, it beats random sampling in all crystals at 4-16 calculations and two-iteration stochastic sampling (sTDEP) in all at eight (supercell basis). On model potentials, the self-consistent form needs 2-16 times fewer calculations than the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation in 13 of 14 cases. With the HSE06 hybrid functional, it is ahead of pooled sTDEP at 4-16 calculations in Si and NaCl, and it gives the thermal expansion of Al within 3% of experiment at 300K. The method has limits: in Al and Si cells of more than 100 atoms, sTDEP is more accurate beyond 4-16 calculations (not so in NaCl up to 16); for dynamically stabilized bcc Zr, the outcome depends on the seed; and above 400 K, the free-energy curvature is not resolved.

title: Multichannel Phonon Interconversion Drives 90 Polarization Rotation for Stable Domain Walls in Hafnium Oxide
abstract: Polarization rotation is a fundamental mechanism in ferroelectric materials, yet how such rotation arises microscopically in fluorite ferroelectrics and gives rise to distinct domain walls (DW) remains unresolved. Phonon modes offer a microscopic route to such structural transformations, as geometric orientations can modify their frequencies, dispersion relations, and vibrational eigenstates when their characteristic wavelengths become comparable to relevant physical dimensions. Here, by combining condensed phonon mode decomposition with first-principles calculations, we investigate the origin of 90 polarization rotation in the ferroelectric phase of HfO2. Using the cubic parent phase as reference, we show that polarization rotation originates from multiple symmetry equivalent phonon modes of distinct eigenstates at different wavevectors in the Brillouin zone, whose coupling and cooperative reorientation continuously evolve to generate distinct 90 Pca21 variants and switching pathways. Among the 90 variants, the lowest-energy switching pathway through the Pmn21 exhibits an energy barrier comparable to, but slightly lower than, that of the 180 polarization reversal pathway through the P42/nmc phase, indicating that 90 polarization rotation is an energetically accessible alternative switching route. We further analyze 90 DW and find that frustrated phonon modes emerge at the wall center, where the coexistence and competition of condensed modes promote local reconfiguration of the lattice distortions, contributing to the elevated DW energies. Importantly, experimental observations with STEM imaging provide direct evidence of atomic mode distortions in stable 90 DW, consistent with the theoretically identified low-energy DW. These findings provide the fundamental structural mechanism underlying 90 switching dynamics, competing domain-wall physics, and macroscopic ferroelectric behavior.

title: Defects and Structural Evolution in CrSBr: Machine-Learning Potentials for Atomistic Simulations
abstract: The layered van der Waals semiconductor CrSBr combines intrinsic magnetic order with semiconducting and optical properties, making it a promising material for multifunctional electronic and photonic applications. Understanding how defects and structural transformations affect its properties under experimentally relevant conditions, however, remains challenging for first-principles simulations due to the relevant length and time scales. Here, we develop and benchmark machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) for the Cr-S-Br system, enabling large-scale atomistic simulations of CrSBr with accuracy approaching that of density functional theory (DFT). The charge-aware variant qNEP achieves near-DFT accuracy in predicting lattice constants, formation enthalpies, vacancy energetics, and the anisotropic pressure response of o-CrSBr. Nudged elastic band calculations reveal that pre-existing S vacancies lower the Cr Frenkel-pair migration barrier by up to 1.1 eV, providing an atomistic mechanism for beam-induced Cr redistribution and structural transformations. Displacement threshold calculations further show that Br is the most susceptible species to electron-beam-induced displacement, identifying the relative ease of removing different atomic species. Together, these results establish a validated computational framework for investigating atomic-scale disorder and structural transformations in CrSBr, providing a basis for defect engineering in materials for future magneto-optoelectronic applications.

title: Variational free complement method with Gaussian expanded complement functions: extensions of general atomic framework including helium and lithium ground states with geminal induced expansion length
abstract: We expand the previous framework of hierarchical-decontraction Gaussian expanded complement functions approach (arXiv: 2603.16262v2) of the free complement (FC) method to $N$-electron atomic systems including general permutations. We consider the possibility that the Gaussian expansion length depends on the presence of the geminal $g$ function. To be more specific, fewer expansion length shall be used when the two-electron $g$ function is combined with the initial wavefunction. The present approach is applied to the ground states of the helium and lithium atoms. The complement function generations via 2s$\rightarrow$1s channel in the lithium ground state are discussed. Symmetries for the associated $N$-electron integrals are analyzed.

title: Quasichemical short-range order in high-entropy reciprocal melts: Li, Na, K‖F, Cl
abstract: We present a combined molecular dynamics and analytical study of quasichemical short-range order and entropy decomposition in the high-entropy reciprocal quaternary melt LiF-NaF-KF-LiCl-NaCl-KCl (equimolar composition Li1/6Na1/6K1/6F1/4Cl1/4) at 900 K. Using a machine-learning interatomic potential trained on ab initio data, we compute all fifteen partial radial distribution functions and the corresponding coordination numbers.

title: FACT frees Ubp10 from nucleosome sequestration after rapid H2B deubiquitination
abstract: Chromatin-modifying enzymes must engage their substrate, act on it and release it, but which step limits their turnover is unclear. Using three-color single-molecule fluorescence, we directly visualized the yeast deubiquitinase Ubp10 removing ubiquitin from H2B on individual nucleosomes. Ubp10 cleaved the mark within seconds of binding, without detectable DNA unwrapping, yet it did not let go: ~80% of nucleosomes remained bound after 45 minutes, and unmodified nucleosomes formed similarly long-lived complexes. Ubp10 turnover is therefore limited by release rather than catalysis. The histone chaperone FACT relieved this bottleneck by accelerating Ubp10-nucleosome dissociation. In living yeast, nuclear depletion of the FACT subunit Spt16 increased the slowly diffusing, chromatin-bound fraction of nucleoplasmic Ubp10. These findings identify FACT-dependent release as a likely mechanism for recycling Ubp10 on chromatin. More broadly, a nucleosome can sequester the enzyme acting on it, making enzyme release a step at which chromatin modification can be controlled.

title: Quantum Embedding from Molecular to Crystalline Environments at the Cost of a Gas-Phase Calculation
abstract: We present a direct-space formulation and implementation of quantum density functional theory (DFT) embedding for molecular active subsystems embedded in frozen environments (hosts) of arbitrary dimensionality, from finite molecular hosts to extended systems. The host is computed once without the embedded molecule (the guest) and is represented only by its electron density fitted in an atom-centered auxiliary Gaussian basis together with its nuclear charges with the periodic electrostatics separated into an explicit near-field and a continuous fast-multipole far-field operator. The method allows the removal of host atoms from this representation to create vacancies or other voids without requiring a supercell creation. Analytic nuclear gradients are also implemented, enabling structural relaxation of the active subsystem. We demonstrate the versatility of the approach through applications to adsorbates on periodic surfaces and molecules embedded in bulk solvent environments. For CO on MgO(001), we show that DFT-in-DFT converges rapidly and reproduces the periodic interaction energy within 0.44 kJ/mol while reducing the cost by a factor of 27. Real-time time-dependent embedded DFT (RT-TDDFET) of methylenecyclopropene in periodic water is showcased to produce a ~0.6 eV solvatochromic blue shift, while strong-field propagation of CO2 on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) yields substrate-induced effects at the cost of a gas-phase propagation. Coupling the embedding scheme to excited-state correlated wave function theory methods such as CC2 yields a solvent shift within 0.01 eV of supermolecular CC2 references, while reducing the computational cost by over 500 times.

title: Kagome Flat Bands from Self-Assembled Water on Non-van der Waals 2D Materials
abstract: The properties of two-dimensional (2D) materials are governed not only by their intrinsic electronic structure but also in particular by their surface chemistry and interactions with the environment. The surfaces of non-van der Waals (non-vdW) 2D materials are intrinsically reactive and may require chemical stabilization under realistic experimental conditions. Here, we perform a systematic first-principles study of water passivation of non-vdW 2D materials and demonstrate that molecular water adsorption is energetically and dynamically favored for a wide range of systems. Rather than dissociating, water molecules frequently remain intact and form adsorbed ordered surface overlayers. These overlayers can adopt a kagome lattice geometry, leading to the emergence of flat electronic bands directly at the valence-band edge. Analysis of the electronic structure reveals a strong intermolecular coupling between neighboring water lone pairs within this kagome topology, while the locked molecular orientations simultaneously produce an electrostatically frustrated surface potential. These findings establish water not only as a stabilizing agent but also as an active element for electronic structure engineering of non-vdW 2D surfaces.

title: Atomically Sharp Magnetic Domain Walls beyond Micromagnetics
abstract: Atomically narrow magnetic domain walls can arise in ultrathin magnetic films, van der Waals magnets, and systems with reduced effective exchange stiffness due to competing exchange interactions. As their width approaches the atomic lattice spacing, the continuum approximation underlying micromagnetics becomes increasingly unreliable. We investigate the structure and stability of such domain walls in a one-dimensional nearest-neighbor J-K-D spin-lattice model incorporating Heisenberg exchange, uniaxial anisotropy, and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI). In the absence of DMI, we demonstrate analytically a continuous transition to an atomically sharp easy-axis wall at the critical exchange-to-anisotropy ratio J/K = 3/2, characterized by the softening of a localized Hessian mode. Atomistic spin-dynamics simulations confirm this transition and reveal that fitting discrete wall profiles with the conventional micromagnetic solution, as commonly done in experimental analyses, underestimates the exchange interaction and overestimates the anisotropy. Finite DMI removes the perfectly collinear wall as a stationary configuration, replacing the transition by a smooth crossover toward a strongly localized but canted wall that approaches the collinear easy-axis configuration only asymptotically in the strong-anisotropy limit. We derive an analytical expression for the DMI-induced canting in this regime and demonstrate its strongly enhanced canting response near the critical ratio. These findings establish the limitations of micromagnetic descriptions of atomically narrow domain walls and suggest opportunities for controlling their structure through anisotropy and DMI.

title: Ultrafast Inter-Aggregate Energy Transfer Drives Efficient Charge Generation in Organic Homojunctions
abstract: Y6-based homojunction organic photovoltaic devices have recently achieved exceptional power conversion efficiencies, surpassing those of conventional organic photovoltaic materials. Although unusually long exciton diffusion lengths and efficient exciton dissociation have been reported, the fundamental mechanism underlying this outstanding performance remains under debate. Here, we report that structurally distinct aggregates in Y6 thin films exhibit complementary charge-transfer (CT) characters that enable directional energy transfer and enhanced exciton delocalization. Using ultrafast spectroscopy, we identify highly efficient Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) between Y6 aggregates, with an ensemble-averaged efficiency of 65% occurring on a sub-picosecond timescale (<1 ps). This aggregate-mediated energy-transfer pathway drives long-range energy migration in Y6 thin films and accounts for the remarkable external quantum efficiencies observed in homojunction devices, even in the absence of conventional donor-acceptor bulk heterojunction morphologies and despite substantial fractions of weak-CT components. Here, using Y6 as a model non-fullerene acceptor (NFA) system, we show that structurally distinct aggregates coexisting in NFA thin films possess complementary CT characters, which are expected to enable directional energy transfer and enhanced exciton delocalization. We establish a general multi-component FRET framework that quantitatively links molecular aggregation, CT character, and excited-state dynamics in systems with multiple packing motifs. This work provides insight into the development of next-generation high-performance organic electronic materials and devices.

title: The ganglioside profile of mouse brain does not respond to changes in dietary n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supply
abstract: Long chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LC-PUFAs) of the n-3 and n-6 families are major components of brain lipids, both in terms of levels and biological significance. They play crucial roles in various neurological processes. The brain is largely dependent on food supply of LC-PUFAs and its lipid composition can be modulated by changes in dietary intake. Sufficient dietary supply of the n-3 LC-PUFAs as well as a balanced n-6/n-3 ratio are required for proper brain development and function.

title: A Mixed Conducting Polymer with pH-Dependent Selectivity for the Oxygen Reduction Reaction
abstract: Achieving 4-electron oxygen reduction with metal-free electrodes has remained a longstanding challenge. Here, we show that poly(benzimidazobenzophenanthroline) (BBL), an n-type ladder polymer, breaks this barrier through an electrocatalytic inner-sphere 2 + 2 series mechanism─a mode of reactivity unprecedented among organic mixed ionic-electronic conductors (OMIECs). Using pH-dependent rotating ring-disk voltammetry, we find that this series mechanism occurs over separate potential windows on BBL.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Plasmon-Defined Chemical Templates for the Nanoscale Assembly of Colloidal Nanoparticles
abstract: Controlling matter with nanoscale spatial selectivity is a key hurdle for plasmonic applications such as nanophotonics, sensing, and catalysis. Plasmon-assisted nanolithography has recently emerged as a powerful strategy to address this challenge by exploiting the highly confined electromagnetic fields and hot carriers generated during plasmon excitation to confine organic or inorganic layers at the nanoscale.

title: Programming supramolecular polymer network topology via homochiral self-sorting
abstract: Stereochemistry greatly influences polymer structure and assembly, yet its use in controlling polymer network topology remains underexplored. Now, homochiral self-sorting is used to suppress primary-loop formation in end-linked polymer networks, offering a strategy for controlling network topology.

title: Structural Insights and Functional Expansion of an Aerobic Skatole Synthase
abstract: SktA from the cyanobacterium Nostoc punctiforme NIES-2108 belongs to the versatile heme oxygenase-like domain-containing nonheme oxidase superfamily, whose natural function is to transform 5-bromotryptophan (5-Br-Trp) to 5-bromoskatole in an oxygen-dependent manner. As SktA is also capable of transforming tryptophan (Trp) to skatole, this enzyme represents a skatole synthase that operates under aerobic conditions. Here, the crystal structure of SktA and its complex with 5-Br-Trp and Trp are reported.

title: Genetically Predicted β-Hydroxybutyrate and Coronary Atherosclerosis: Mendelian Randomization and APOE-Associated Transcriptomic Signatures in Human Atherosclerotic Plaques
abstract: AimsKetone bodies are implicated in cardiovascular metabolism, yet the contributions of β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), acetoacetate and acetone to coronary atherosclerosis remain unclear.MethodsWe integrated Mendelian randomization (MR), cross-trait GWAS analysis, ApoE pQTL-MR and colocalization to investigate genetic associations with coronary atherosclerosis, complemented by bulk transcriptomic analysis, machine learning-based signature construction, immune infiltration analysis and single-cell analysis to characterize APOE-associated molecular features in human atherosclerotic…

title: Low-Scaling Equation-of-Motion Coupled Cluster Method for Open-Shell Systems: I. IP-EOM-DLPNO-CCSD
abstract: We present the formulation and implementation of an unrestricted/open-shell domain-based local pair natural orbital equation-of-motion coupled-cluster method with single and double excitations for vertical ionization potentials (UHF IP-EOM-DLPNO-CCSD). The method extends the open-shell DLPNO–CCSD reference calculation to the (N – 1)-electron sector by reusing the localized occupied orbitals, pair domains, pair lists, and pair natural orbital spaces generated for the correlated ground state. Removal of an α or β electron is treated in separate spin sectors. The one-hole sector is retained in the fully localized occupied space, whereas the two-hole–one-particle sector is represented in compact, spin-resolved PNO spaces. The accuracy is controlled by the standard LoosePNO, NormalPNO, and TightPNO hierarchy. For ionized states dominated by one-hole character, canonical and local calculations performed with the same quasi-restricted-orbital (QRO) reference give typical RMSD differences of a few hundredths of an eV for the main-group radical and transition-metal benchmark sets. A representative TightPNO comparison for naphthalene further indicates that the additional local IP-EOM approximation contributes less than 0.10 eV for the ten matched states examined. Larger delocalized systems show less regular threshold dependence, and even predominantly one-hole states can exhibit changes greater than 0.1 eV between NormalPNO and TightPNO. Timing calculations for anionic acenes up to heptacene, with 1038 basis functions, show low-order effective scaling for the IP-EOM step. Applications to C70– and to the Pheophytin radical anion, the latter containing 3020 basis functions, demonstrate that the method can treat large open-shell molecular systems beyond the size range routinely accessible to canonical IP-EOM-CCSD. Finally, comparisons with available experimental data for the N-carbazolyl radical and the ovalene radical cation provide additional context for the calculated vertical ionization energies.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: FermiLink: An Agent Harness for Multidomain Scientific Simulations
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agent harnesses have been developed for autonomous scientific simulations, but most current agent harnesses are tested on a single or a small set of software packages. Herein, FermiLink, an extensible open-source agent harness, is introduced for multidomain scientific simulations. Its key design principle is the separation of package knowledge bases from simulation workflows, so that simulation workflows in FermiLink, from figure-level simulations to full-paper-level research on high-performance computing clusters, operate uniformly among supported packages via a…
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: Exploring Charge Distribution and Rate Variation in LiNi0.8Mn0.1Co0.1O2/LiMn0.7Fe0.3PO4 Blends for High Rate Electrodes
abstract: Composite electrodes containing physical mixtures (“blends”) of multiple active materials have generated commercial interest for lithium battery applications due to the possibility of enhanced electrochemical performance, which are not fully characterised. This investigation uses mixtures of well-known LiMn0.7Fe0.3PO4 (LMFP) and LiNi0.8Mn0.1Co0.1O2 (NMC) materials as a model blend system to investigate rate- and composition-dependent effects on performance. A combination of electrochemical and operando techniques reveals that deviations in performance with respect to the linear combination of the component materials originate from uneven current distribution, leading to different effective rates between components and spontaneous lithium-ion redistribution, commonly termed the “buffer effect”. Results of experiments using a specially adapted three-electrode setup show that the effective rates of the components vary considerably depending on the cell state of charge, with much higher effective rates being reached than the applied cell rate. The same setup allows the direction of lithium redistribution to be visualised when the system relaxes following a current pulse, and this directionality also varies with cell state of charge. Electrochemical investigations and Raman spectra reveal that blending reduces chemical sensitivity to ambient storage conditions and leads to reduced degradation by forming a protective LMFP layer around the more reactive NMC particles. Operando data shows that the blend components evolve largely as expected when taking into account their specific effective rates, in line with the materials retaining their individual electrochemical properties. This study highlights the importance of considering relative windows of electrochemical activity when selecting blend components and paves the way for future optimisation of electrode blends for high rate lithium-ion batteries.

title: Molecular traps reveal limitations of synthesis planning algorithms
abstract: Computer-aided synthesis planning (CASP) has advanced substantially over the past decade. However, gains on conventional metrics do not mean that algorithms have truly mastered comprehensive chemical knowledge or can deliver practical routes with high yield and high selectivity. In real synthetic settings, chemists must contend with key chemical constraints such as chemoselectivity, regioselectivity and steric hindrance.

title: Internal Free Volume Directs Hydration-Induced Amorphization of Hollow α-V2O5
abstract: Hollow particles are designed to keep their cavities open, but a cavity can also be consumed as a structural resource. Thin-walled hollow α-V2O5 converts in aqueous ZnSO4 at 80 °C into a filled, hydrated, amorphous phase, Zn0.23(OH)0.46V2O5·1.0H2Oa charge-balanced composition from ICP-OES and TGA that assumes V5+ and hydroxide compensation of the zinc. Electron tomography shows the cavity disappearing as the particle grows from 246 to about 420 nm, with 6% of the vanadium lost to solution. The hollow shell takes up three times the water of commercial V2O5.

title: Dual-reporter assay for selective small molecule inhibition of expanded toxic huntingtin
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expansion of CAG repeats in exon 1 of the human huntingtin gene (HTT). The resultant pathogenic allele (mHTT) produces a mutant huntingtin protein (mHtt) containing an expanded polyglutamine tract. Because mHtt drives neurodegeneration while wildtype huntingtin (Htt) remains critical for regulation of gene transcription and cell survival, an ideal therapeutic would specifically downregulate mHtt expression while preserving Htt. Small molecules are attractive candidates for HD given their ability to penetrate the blood-brain barrier and amenability to oral dosing, but there remains no high-throughput platform that reports both efficacy and allele selectivity. Here, we present a bacterial assay in which exon 1 of HTT and mHTT, each fused to spectrally distinct fluorescent proteins, are co-expressed in the same cell, allowing simultaneous quantification of their expression in the presence of small molecules. This high-throughput assay isolates the effect of small molecules on huntingtin expression without confounding factors present in mammalian cells, such as endogenous Htt or human RNA-binding proteins. To validate this assay, we evaluated two previously reported CAG repeat binding compounds and used circular dichroism spectroscopy and cell-free protein synthesis to investigate their underlying mechanisms. Furamidine exhibited reproducible, sequence-dependent effects, altering the structural stability of HTT RNA and selectively decreasing the wildtype Htt expression (a selectivity profile opposite to what is therapeutically required). In contrast, myricetin did not affect HTT RNA stability and its decreased signal in the dual-expression assay was due to fluorophore artifacts. This highlights the importance of complementary workflows in distinguishing genuine modulators from reporter-specific artifacts. Collectively, these findings establish the dual-expression assay as a screening platform for CAG repeat-targeting small molecules and demonstrate the importance of determining which allele reported compounds preferentially affect.

title: Mapping the reactive cysteine landscape of the NOD-like receptor pyrin domain-containing 3 protein
abstract: NOD-like receptor pyring-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) is a cytosolic pattern recognition receptor that drives assembly of an oligomeric inflammasome complex to stimulate pro-inflammatory cytokine production and pyroptotic cell death. Extensive research has shown that NLRP3 activation is dependent on intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS). Despite this, the precise targets of ROS in this process remain undefined. In this study, a combination of chemoproteomics, in vitro biochemical assays and molecular dynamics simulations were used to characterize reactive Cys and how they may impact NLRP3 conformation and activity status. Affinity-captured NLRP3 was subjected to reverse-thiol trapping to reveal a pool of reactive Cys residues that were identified in subsequent chemoproteomic analyses. C150, C196, and C884 were consistently detected with both in vitro and in cellulo experiments. Several NLRP3 mutants were generated; C150A and C196A (NACHT domain) as well as C933A and C941A (LRR domain) reduced IL-1b output in a reconstituted inflammasome assay. Molecular simulation of Cys sulfenylation in the LRR suggests structural alterations that reposition the trLRR loop to destabilize the inactive NLRP3 structure. Structural modelling provided insights for how Cys oxidation of the LRR may impact on NLRP3 structure. Collectively, the results establish a mechanistic understanding for how ROS may promote NLRP3 inflammasome activation.

title: Cisplatin-triggered sensory dysfunction in NER-defective C. elegans involves GABAergic and cholinergic signaling
abstract: Cisplatin (CisPt) is a widely used anticancer drug that causes neurotoxicity as a dose-limiting adverse effect. DNA damage contributes to CisPt-induced neurotoxicity, yet the molecular mechanisms involved remain unclear. Here, we aim to identify pathophysiological mechanisms contributing to DNA damage-driven development of sensory neuronal dysfunction using the 3R-compliant model organism Caenorhabditis elegans.

title: DIALECT: DNA-Programmable Synthetic Cells Communicate with Mammalian Cells through Synthetic Receptors
abstract: Synthetic cells can regulate mammalian signalling through the controlled release of diffusible protein ligands, but coupling programmable synthetic-cell senders to orthogonal, engineered mammalian receptors remains challenging. Here we present DIALECT (DNA-Instructed Assembly of Ligands for Engineered Cellular Transduction), a platform in which proteinosome-based synthetic cells translate sequence-defined DNA inputs into coiled-coil signalling ligand outputs for engineered mammalian receptors.

title: Nanomechanical phenotyping uncovers a non-canonical smooth muscle-like hypercontractility program in lung squamous cell carcinoma myofibroblasts
abstract: Myofibroblast-like cancer-associated fibroblasts (myCAFs) drive the stiff, tumor-promoting microenvironment, yet their mechanical phenotype in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains undefined. myCAFs from major NSCLC subtypes (lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC)) were examined combining atomic force microscopy and traction force microscopy with molecular and signaling analyses. LUAD-myCAFs displayed canonical myofibroblast features, including elevated stiffness, traction forces, ROCK-MYPT1 signaling, and -SMA-rich stress fibers.

title: Engineering Nanobody Conformational Switches
abstract: Conformational signaling is widely used in biology, but remains difficult to engineer into proteins. Here, we explore ligand-induced folding of nanobodies as a general strategy to generate conformational receptors for a broad range of target ligands. More specifically, we have generated partially unfolded nanobody variants that fold exclusively upon binding to their target ligand. To do so, we have introduced destabilizing mutations in the framework region, carefully tuning their stability while preserving molecular recognition. Given the high conservation of the framework across different nanobodies, this approach is broadly applicable to many other target ligands, which has enabled us to engineer conformational switches for three different important biomarkers and drugs: the pregnancy hormone chorionic gonadotropin, the cytokine tumor necrosis factor alpha, and the chemotherapy and immunosuppressant drug methotrexate. Another useful property of conformational signaling is that it can directly gate signal transduction, which we have leveraged to build an optical sensor for the quantitative detection of the pregnancy hormone in urine. Finally, conformational signaling introduces new mechanisms for the allosteric modulation of binding, which we have explored to control the affinity and dynamic range of the sensor. Our work thus establishes a rational strategy for engineering conformational signaling receptors with customizable properties and generalizable for many different target ligands.

title: Positive cooperativity enhances coupling of a second G protein to a GPCR dimer
abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are cell surface integral membrane proteins that transduce environmental, hormonal and neurotransmitter molecular signals into intracellular responses. Here we studied a class D1 fungal receptor, Ste2, an obligate dimer that couples two G proteins per dimer and show that coupling of the second G protein has an 18-fold higher affinity than coupling of the first. The molecular mechanism uncovered suggests that coupling of the first G protein to one protomer stabilizes the adjacent protomer in an active conformation with a pre-formed G protein coupling site, thus increasing the affinity for coupling of the second G protein. Protomer-based stabilization of an adjacent protomer in a unique conformational state within a dimer may represent a general mechanism by which oligomerization alters GPCR pharmacology.

title: π-SPECFormer: A Mass Spectrometry-based Foundation Model for Decoding the Dark Proteome
abstract: In mass-spectrometry–based proteomics, a substantial proportion of acquired spectra remain unidentified, concealing a vast reservoir of biological variations commonly termed the "dark proteome", potentially obscuring sequence mutations, non–canonical peptides and post–translational modifications. Existing deep-learning methods largely rely on supervised training with peptide–spectrum matches (PSMs), limiting their ability to learn from the much larger pool of unannotated spectra.

title: S. pombe Mto1:Mto2 stabilizes γ-tubulin positions within the γ-TuRC
abstract: Microtubules are present in all eukaryotes and are nucleated by multiprotein {gamma}-tubulin ring complexes ({gamma}-TuRCs), ring-shaped structures that contain several copies of the {gamma}-tubulin small complex ({gamma}-TuSC). {gamma}-TuRCs nucleate microtubules via a template-based mechanism in which the positions of {gamma}-tubulins in the {gamma}-TuSCs match the position of {gamma}-tubulin dimers in the microtubule lattice. Although {gamma}-TuSC proteins are highly conserved, other components of the {gamma}-TuRC can vary in different organisms, as can their relative importance. Here, we characterize two different simplified {gamma}-TuRCs from fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, using recombinant purified proteins and negative stain electron microscopy. We show that a nucleation-incompetent {gamma}-TuRC that contains only {gamma}-TuSC proteins plus the microprotein Mzt1 ({gamma}-TuSC:Mzt1) can form rings as efficiently as a large, nucleation-competent complex (MGM) that additionally contains the proteins Mto1 and Mto2. We find that the position of {gamma}-tubulins in {gamma}-TuSC:Mzt1 are less well defined than in MGM. Comparative modelling using our electron microscopy and crosslinking mass spectrometry data, together with structures of {gamma}-TuRCs from other organisms, suggests that Mto1 and Mto2 form a multimeric outer mantle surrounding the {gamma}-TuSC:Mzt1 {gamma}-TuRC. This mantle may stabilize positions of {gamma}-tubulins within MGM, explaining the microtubule-nucleating ability of MGM and highlighting the diversity of non-{gamma}-TuSC proteins in modulating {gamma}-TuRC structure and function.

title: Cationic Ionomer Coatings Promote Anion Electroreduction: Nitrate Reduction as a Model Reaction
abstract: Electrolysis technologies represent a promising pathway to valorize abundant feedstocks using renewable electricity. While ionomers serve critical roles as ion conductors and catalyst binders in electrolyzers, their impact on electrochemical transformations of ionic species remains poorly understood compared to extensively studied neutral-molecule conversions like water splitting and CO2 reduction. Herein, we use the electrochemical nitrate reduction reaction as a model transformation to investigate the influence of ionomer coatings in anion electroreduction reactions, which face fundamental challenges from electrostatic anion depletion near negatively polarized cathodes and premature desorption of anionic intermediates. We demonstrate that cationic ionomer coatings increase local nitrate concentration up to 10-fold compared to bulk electrolyte due to the interfacial Donnan potential. While prior studies have shown that ionomers can influence the local reaction microenvironment, this work provides, to the best of our knowledge, the first quantitative measurement of nitrate concentration within ionomer coatings as a function of charge density and its impact on catalysis. A 5-fold enhancement in ammonium partial current density was achieved with the ionomer bearing the highest charge density. Using in situ attenuated total reflectance surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS), we quantified enhanced local nitrate concentration (up to 1.1 M versus 0.1 M in bulk electrolyte), conversion, and supply with increasing charge density. This study establishes guiding principles for tuning ionomer charge identity and density to control interfacial ion concentrations in electrochemical transformations of dilute charged substrates.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Broadband RF Design with MEEP: A Set of 3D-Printed Open-Source RF Horns in the multi-GHz Bandwidth
abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) antenna design and fabrication traditionally proceeds in three phases. First, the design performance is modeled with expensive, proprietary software. Second, the design is built using precision metal machining or printed circuit board (PCB) fabrication. Third, the result is characterized using RF measurement tools. The process can include machine learning for optimization.

title: Spin-State-Selective Secondary-Sphere Control in Hemicryptophane Cages Enables Tunable Reactivity of Iron-Oxo Centers
abstract: High-valent iron-oxo species are key intermediates in oxidation catalysis, yet modulating their electronic structures via the secondary coordination sphere remains challenging. Here, we designed a hemicryptophane-encapsulated iron-oxo complex (FeO-TPA@Hm2) and elucidate how the cage modulates methane C–H activation. Our calculations indicate that the Hm2 framework stabilizes the quintet state as the global minimum, potentially increasing the accessibility of the low-barrier quintet pathway. Crucially, we further uncover a spin-gated regulatory mechanism: on the triplet manifold, the cage exhibits pronounced redox noninnocence, acting as a tunable electron reservoir where remote substituents ″switch″ the electronic topology among Fe(III)–O2–, Fe(III)–O–•, Fe(IV)═O, and Fe(II)–O•• regimes. In contrast, the quintet state displays remarkable electronic rigidity due to exchange stabilization, rendering the cage effectively redox-innocent. Consequently, although the triplet surface is highly sensitive to substituent-induced polarization, the quintet pathway remains robust and dominant. This work establishes a synergy between spin-selective reactivity and spin-differentiated substituent sensitivity, providing a programmable strategy for orchestrating electron-transfer pathways in supramolecular catalysis.

title: Chemistry in Pictures: Golden tears
Accelerating CO2 Biocatalysis through Multimodal AI-Guided Enzyme Prioritization and Spatial Confinement
abstract: Direct biological conversion of CO2 into value-added chemicals is severely restricted by sluggish enzyme kinetics and inefficient intracellular carbon flux. Here, we address these catalytic bottlenecks by synergizing multimodal deep learning, mechanistic enzyme engineering, and synthetic organelle assembly. Using CASKP, a TransKP-guided candidate-prioritization framework that integrates sequence representations with a docking-derived scalar feature, we prioritized and experimentally identified a highly active β-carbonic anhydrase, PbCA, for improving intracellular CO2 supply.

title: PP271, a novel bacteriophage primase-polymerase, enables Primer-Free DNA Amplification
abstract: Primases are essential enzymes that initiate DNA replication by synthesizing de novo primers for replicative DNA polymerases, which ensure accurate genome duplication owing to their high specificity, fidelity, and processivity. PrimPols have emerged as versatile DNA-initiating enzymes that are widely distributed across diverse replication systems, from bacteriophages to humans. In this work, a novel PrimPol enzyme, PP271, encoded by bacteriophage vB-EfaS-271, was characterized.

title: Bacterial major vault protein homologs form divergent vault structures
abstract: Vaults are large, enigmatic macromolecular protein complexes composed of symmetrically arranged major vault protein (MVP) subunits with a wide variety of proposed functions. While MVP is conserved in most eukaryotes, its prevalence in other domains of life has not been well studied. Furthermore, whether bacterial MVP homologs assemble into vaults remains unknown. Here, we identify and examine a subset of bacterial MVP homologs and report cryoEM structures of an intact vault from Corallococcus praedator and a half-vault from a Deltaproteobacteria bacterium. Both bacterial vault complexes exhibit architectures unlike any other previously characterized vault with barrel/cap symmetries of D35/C13 and C48/C16, respectively. These data demonstrate that bacterial MVP homologs can assemble into vault structures and highlight the structural diversity of vaults across domains of life.

title: Decoupling Quantification and Identification for Label-Free Top-Down Proteomics Improves Proteome Coverage
abstract: Quantifying proteoforms is essential for understanding biological processes. The most widely used quantification approach in top-down proteomics (TDP) is label-free quantification (LFQ), where quantification and identification compete for acquisition time. We identified missing values, insufficient fragmentation, and undersampling of low-abundance proteoforms as major factors limiting conventional TDP-LFQ workflows. Our proposed workflow decouples quantification and identification through MS1-only quantification followed by targeted data-dependent MS2 identification. The MS1-only acquisition more than doubled the number of mass features quantified reliably and improved quantification precision. Focusing targeted MS2 acquisition on significantly differentially abundant features enables optimization of MS2 parameters and increases identification coverage by 50%. The workflow was validated across different chromatographic conditions, MS acquisition setups, and sample preparation strategies. In Escherichia coli grown on glucose or acetate, the increased depth enabled by this workflow revealed biological insights inaccessible to a previously published bottom-up proteomics dataset. Overall, decoupling quantification and identification improves quantitative depth and proteoform coverage in TDP-LFQ and provides a flexible strategy for high-sensitivity and high-throughput proteoform quantification.

title: Phosphorylation-dependent conformational change in the Keratin 19 head domain: Implications for filament assembly and binding to GSK3β and 14-3-3
abstract: Keratins are intermediate filament (IF) proteins expressed in various cell types, playing a crucial role in mechanical support and signaling pathways. Keratin 19 (K19) is predominantly found in gut epithelia and early embryonic ectoderm. K19 interacts with signaling proteins such as GSK3{beta} and 14-3-3 to participate in cell signaling pathways. However, details on the binding sites of these proteins on K19, and specific molecular mechanisms governing these interactions, are lacking. Additionally, the N-terminal head domains of IFs including K19 are considered intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), and their atomic-resolution structures are unavailable. Using NMR spectroscopy, we obtained the first solution structures of K19 head domain peptides. Structural models involving phosphomimetic peptides suggest a phosphorylation-dependent conformational change in the K19 head domain. The phosphomimetic S35E substitution alters the conformation of the head domain, affecting its association with keratin filaments and K19-binding partners. NMR spectral changes indicate that the S35E substitution affects the association of the K19 head domain to K8/K19 filaments and GSK3{beta}, whereas no significant binding changes were observed with 14-3-3{zeta} and 14-3-3{sigma}. Cell-based analyses further showed that the S35E mutation altered keratin filament organization and reduced the proximity between K19 and GSK3{beta} in 293T cells, whereas no significant change was observed in the proximity between K19 and 14-3-3{sigma}. Our findings provide insight into the structure-function relationship of the head domains in IF proteins with direct implications for the assembly of filaments and their role in signal modulation.

title: Stable training and confidence‑calibrated generation of urinary stone CT images via physics‑constrained GANs under small‑sample conditions
abstract: In recent years, artificial intelligence has become integral to modern medicine. Deep learning algorithms are widely used to assist clinical diagnosis, and medical image synthesis has become increasingly mature. However, in small-sample scenarios, synthetic images often overlook infrequent but clinically valuable lesion features. To address the challenges of training instability, insufficient authenticity, and limited clinical usability, we propose a two-stage framework based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs).

title: Multitask Deep Learning for Joint Deepfake Speech Detection and Spoofing Attack Attribution
abstract: The rapid advancement of neural speech synthesis and voice conversion technologies has increased the realism of synthetic speech, creating significant challenges for biometric authentication and digital forensics. This study proposes a Multi-Task Deep Learning (MT-DL) framework that jointly addresses binary deepfake speech detection and supervised spoof attribution of known attack classes.

title: Redefining Synovial Pathotypes in Psoriatic Arthritis through Multi-Modal Histology and Machine Learning (The PSYNOVIUM Study)
abstract: Background Synovial inflammation in psoriatic arthritis (PsA) lacks a validated histological classification framework. Current approaches apply rheumatoid arthritis (RA) synovial pathotypes to PsA, which overlooks immunobiological differences between the diseases and limits the predictive power of tissue stratification. We aimed to define data-driven, PsA-specific synovial pathotypes to facilitate tissue-driven precision medicine.

title: Alternative approach could reduce reliance on potentially toxic surfactants in pharmaceutical and food applications
abstract: An international research team led by the University of Sydney has found a way to formulate microemulsions without traditional surfactants, which are often toxic and hard to separate from end products. The findings have important implications for pharmaceutical applications and food additives.

title: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Radical Dearomatization of Electrophilic Heterocyclic and Non-Heterocyclic Arenes
abstract: Catalytic asymmetric dearomatization provides a powerful strategy for converting readily available aromatic feedstocks into valuable three-dimensional molecular scaffolds. Despite substantial advances over the past several decades, general methods for catalytic asymmetric dearomatization of electrophilic arenes, particularly non-heterocyclic substrates with high aromatic stabilization energies, remain a challenging task. Here, we report the use of a hydrogen atom transfer mechanism for biocatalytic radical dearomatization of electron-deficient arenes. Repurposing and directed evolution of our previously developed P450 halogen atom transferases furnished hydrogen atom transfer dearomatases that catalyze the stereoselective dearomatization of a range of electrophilic arenes, including electron-deficient indoles, pyrroles, and simple benzene derivatives. These evolved biocatalysts facilitated both diastereodivergent and enantiodivergent radical dearomatization, providing access to fused and spirocyclic chiral scaffolds bearing challenging quaternary and/or contiguous stereocenters. Computational and experimental studies revealed that a strategically positioned active-site lysine residue enables enzyme-controlled proton transfer against the intrinsic thermodynamic stereopreference, allowing catalyst-controlled reversal of diastereoselectivity from a common radical intermediate. Importantly, the evolved dearomatases efficiently transformed challenging arene substrates that proved recalcitrant under previously optimized Fe, Mn and Co-based metal-hydride hydrogen atom transfer conditions. Collectively, these results establish new-to-nature metalloredox biocatalysis as a powerful strategy for overcoming longstanding challenges in asymmetric radical catalysis.

title: OriDynamics: Towards a World Model for Biomolecular Dynamics
abstract: Biomolecular recognition and regulation depend on atomic interactions that change as molecular partners fluctuate and adopt alternative conformations. Modeling these processes requires ensembles that capture both conformational diversity and coordinated atomic fluctuations between interacting molecules. Here we present OriDynamics, a unified framework for all-atom ensemble generation across protein monomers and complexes with small molecules or protein partners. OriDynamics introduces a latent ensemble decomposition that couples broad conformational exploration in a compact structural latent space with local all-atom sampling around generated proposals. Ensemble-level supervision constrains mean positions, fluctuation amplitudes and joint coordinate covariance to capture coordinated atomic variability within and between molecular partners. Across benchmarks of proteins and their complexes, OriDynamics demonstrates superior overall performance in conformational coverage, atomic fluctuation fidelity and interaction geometry compared with leading baselines. Application studies further demonstrate recovery of alternative functional conformations and partner-dependent changes in conformational ensembles alongside sampling of configurations associated with ligand dissociation. These capabilities provide a foundation for a biomolecular world model that represents accessible molecular states and their dependence on interaction context.

title: Trajectory Density Ratios under Weak Support: A Survey across the Sciences
abstract: Many problems across the sciences compare two stochastic processes through the sequences they generate. Reinforcement learning asks what a new policy would return from the trajectories of an old one; molecular simulation asks how much more a ligand binds from samples of the unbound state; climate attribution asks how a heat wave shifted under warming; and language-model post-training asks what a deployed agent will do from logged interactions. In every case, one quantity would answer all these questions at once: the ratio of the two probability laws over their generated sequences, the trajectory density ratio. This ratio exists only under strong conditions. When one process reaches states the other cannot, the ratio does not exist; when their overlap is thin, its variance grows without control with the sequence length; and when they concentrate on different lower-dimensional sets, the ratio is undefined altogether. Weak support of this kind is the norm for sequence data, not a sampling accident, and its price is paid in identifiability rather than in noise alone. This survey organizes the field around a three-level diagnosis of weak support and a map of the nine retreats that methods take when the full ratio is out of reach, from direct estimation and reweighting through staged decomposition, stationarization, and partial-identification bounds to smoothing, transport couplings, operator spectra, and direct estimation of a single functional. Each retreat keeps part of what the ratio offers and pays for the rest, and each application domain has standardized the retreat its data force. The survey closes with open problems: testable diagnostics at every level, partial identification at the trajectory level, a rate theory of time-amplified error, and benchmarks with ground truth.

title: HyInv Technical Report
abstract: Inverse folding designs amino-acid sequences for a given protein backbone, and screening needs many candidates that are both diverse and well folded. We present HyInv, a 1.96-million-parameter backbone-conditioned graph network with an encoder-decoder architecture, trained by Hyra 2.0, the research agent developed by our team: pretrained with random-order autoregressive sequence modeling, followed by structure-reward reinforcement learning. At inference, a grouped draft-and-rewrite sampler that uses separate draft and rewrite temperatures improves refolding TM-score at matched diversity. An optimized implementation with BF16 numerics designs 128 sequences for a 402-residue backbone in 50.6 ms on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU, about 52 times faster than the reference sampler, and an exact FP32 path that returns the reference sequences is 8.7 times faster. Across five benchmark datasets and seven dataset-predictor combinations, HyInv reaches a higher average scTM than all ten external baselines at comparable or higher sequence diversity, with large margins over ProteinMPNN and ProteinZero V2. The same default setting supports de novo backbones, pocket-constrained libraries, enzyme redesign with the catalytic site kept, and loop redesign. We have released our code and model at https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hyra-results/tree/main/AI4Science/hyinv.

title: Structural Insights into the Coaggregation Mechanism of TTR and TDP
abstract: The self-aggregation of TTR and TDP proteins is closely associated with the treatment of TDP-43 proteinopathies. Recent experimental evidence suggests that TTR and TDP-43 can coaggregate in the cytoplasm of Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) patients and disease models. However, their coaggregation molecular mechanisms are unknown. Herein, we investigated the conformational ensembles of TTR, TDP, and TTR-TDP systems, respectively, employing all-atom replica exchange molecular dynamics (REMD), molecular dynamics (MD), and coarse grain (CG) MD simulation methods.
venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling

title: CheMeleon model adapts to predict molecular properties from scant data
abstract: Discovering new molecules for specific uses is a major driver of progress in a wide variety of industries, whether it's pharmaceutical companies looking for new drugs or electronics or energy companies seeking new materials with particular properties. But it's also largely a trial-and-error process, because there is not yet any way to perfectly predict how a given chemical compound will behave in terms of the myriad different properties and responses materials can exhibit.

title: Severity-Controlled Prediction Sets for Medication Recommendation
abstract: Medication recommendation is a multi-label prediction task. However, existing prediction-set evaluation and calibration methods rely mainly on exact-overlap metrics and therefore treat all missed medications as equally severe, overlooking how closely the prediction set matches them within the medication hierarchy. To address this, we introduce Conformal Severity Control (CSC), a post-hoc framework for calibrating medication prediction sets under hierarchy-aware mismatch severity. CSC uses the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) hierarchy to quantify mismatch severity and controls patient-level severity without retraining the predictor, supporting both average severity and upper-quantile severity for the highest-severity mismatches. Experiments on MIMIC-IV show that CSC tracks user-specified severity tolerances and shifts prediction sets away from distant mismatches toward exact or close matches.

title: MOTIF: LLM-Defined Material Taxonomies for OOD Property Prediction via Invariant Feature Selection
abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization remains a central challenge in materials property prediction, where models must extrapolate to novel chemistries beyond the training distribution. While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong scientific reasoning, their direct use for quantitative prediction remains limited. To address this, we systematically evaluate multiple roles for LLM assistance, finding that only taxonomy-based grouping consistently improves OOD generalization over a strong kNN+GBT baseline. Building on this, we here propose MOTIF, a framework that leverages LLMs not as predictors, but as generators of candidate taxonomies that partition materials into chemically meaningful environments. These taxonomies are evaluated via training-only pseudo-OOD validation, and only those that improve generalization are retained. Invariant feature selection is then applied within each accepted taxonomy, followed by gated aggregation across taxonomies. We evaluate on 2D halide perovskites, where bandgap prediction must generalize across distinct organic spacer families. On this benchmark, MOTIF reduces mean OOD MAE from 0.122 to 0.111 eV. Under a frozen dev/test protocol, the deployable configuration further improves errors from 0.123 to 0.117 eV (electronic bandgap) and from 0.181 to 0.173 eV (optical bandgap). Beyond this primary task, we validate transferability across additional materials datasets, including 3D perovskite solar cell efficiencies and Matbench benchmarks with structure-based splits. Across domains, MOTIF consistently improves robustness under distribution shift, outperforming expert-defined groupings, rule-based heuristics, and clustering baselines, while remaining competitive with strong classical selection methods. These results demonstrate that LLMs are most effective not as predictors, but as tools for discovering structure in data.

title: MOOD: Benchmarking Post-Hoc OOD Detection for Materials Property Prediction
abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is essential for deploying machine learning models in high stakes scientific applications, yet methods that flag OOD inputs without retraining the model have been validated almost exclusively on image classification. We introduce MOOD (Materials Out-of-Distribution Detection), a benchmark for evaluating whether these post-hoc OOD detectors transfer to graph neural networks (GNNs) on materials property prediction. MOOD evaluates 15 post-hoc detectors and 2 supervised diagnostic probes across 4 GNN architectures, 5 MatBench tasks, and 15 physically motivated compositional and structural shifts, yielding 264 evaluation settings and over 13,000 AUROC measurements across three encoder training seeds. Our evaluation reveals three key findings. First, current post-hoc detectors perform near chance; all 15 detectors achieve an AUROC around 0.5. Second, detector failures decompose into two regimes: method bottlenecks and encoder bottlenecks. Method bottlenecks arise when supervised probes can separate in-distribution (ID) from OOD samples but unsupervised detectors fail, meaning that the embeddings contain OOD signal that current detectors do not extract. Encoder bottlenecks arise when even supervised probes fail to separate ID from OOD samples, indicating that the relevant shift is not accessible in the frozen GNN representation. Third, when OOD prediction error exceeds ID error, the AUROC of distance-based and density-based detectors correlates with the size of that gap. Collectively, these findings indicate that reliable OOD detection in scientific domains requires representation learning strategies that explicitly preserve OOD relevant signal, particularly for tasks where current GNN architectures encode no extractable signal at all.

title: Operator Learning of Microstructure-Dependent Internal-Variable Models for Inelastic Homogenization: Approximation and Complexity
abstract: We study the learning of homogenized constitutive laws for inelastic heterogeneous materials, aiming to replace costly concurrent unit-cell simulations with surrogates that generalize across loading histories and microstructures. We focus on the recurrent neural operator framework, motivated by the explicit form of homogenized Kelvin--Voigt linear viscoelasticity. In this framework, internal variables enable a Markovian approximation of loading-history dependence, and neural operators represent the microstructure-dependent constitutive response. For periodic Kelvin--Voigt viscoelasticity, we prove a universal approximation theorem showing that the model can approximate the homogenized constitutive law to any prescribed accuracy, uniformly in time and over a wide set of admissible strain trajectories and microstructural property fields, in two and three dimensions. This comprises a significant extension of the existing, somewhat limited, one-dimensional theory that uses explicit solutions for piecewise constant materials. Instead, in two and three dimensions, we adopt a more versatile approximation based on the spectral representation of the memory kernel that arises from homogenization. This also enables us to give an explicit bound on the internal-variable dimension, sufficient for approximation, exhibiting logarithmic growth in the inverse relative stress error and in material contrast. Numerical experiments on viscoelasticity and crystal plasticity complement the theory, illustrating the roles of internal-variable dimension and sample complexity in learning homogenized responses from unit-cell data. Theoretical results are formally verified in Lean 4.

title: A Deformulating Multi-Attribute SEC Method for Simultaneous Quantification of Total RNA, Conjugated Antibody, and Free Antibody in Targeted Lipid Nanoparticles
abstract: Targeted lipid nanoparticles (tLNPs) hold promise for improving cell- and tissue-selective delivery of therapeutic payloads but introduce analytical challenges associated with characterizing both encapsulated cargo and surface-associated targeting ligands within the same formulation. Conventional nucleic acid and protein assays can be affected by nanoparticle scattering, matrix interference, or a limited ability to distinguish conjugated antibody from free antibody.

title: BFEE3: An AI-Assisted, Feature-Rich, and Streamlined Platform for Absolute Binding Free Energy Calculations
abstract: Absolute binding free energy (ABFE) calculations for protein–ligand and protein–protein complexes, based on molecular simulations, are now established as essential tools in drug design and protein engineering. Nevertheless, both geometrical and alchemical routes require multistage simulation campaigns involving input preparation, postprocessing, and bookkeeping. These complex procedures can introduce preventable errors and limit accessibility for nonexpert practitioners. Therefore, there is a clear need for user-friendly and automated software environments to address these challenges.
venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling

title: Meta-Analysis Studies on Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: A Bibliometric Analysis (2010-2025)
abstract: Aim Meta-analyses of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare have proliferated across many clinical domains, yet no study has mapped this literature as a body of scholarship in its own right. This study aims to conduct a bibliometric analysis of meta-analysis studies on AI in healthcare published between 2010 and 2025. Methods Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 646 research and review articles indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus databases (2010–2025) were analyzed for citation patterns, annual trends, and leading countries, institutions, authors, publishers, and…

title: Fully automated solid-phase extraction and edge-deployed spectroscopy-based machine learning platform for on-site detection of PFOS/PFOA in industrial wastewater
abstract: Rapid on-site screening of perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) in industrial wastewater is hindered by matrix interference, laborious pretreatment, and reliance on laboratory instrumentation. Here, we developed a portable device integrating automated solid-phase extraction, fluorescence detection using poly(3-alkylthiophenes) (P3ATs), and principal component analysis-support vector machine (PCA-SVM) classification within a 30-min workflow. Performance was evaluated using samples from three fluorochemical wastewater streams.

title: A Chiral Photoactive Ligand for Enantioconvergent Nickel-Catalyzed C(sp 2 )–C(sp 3 ) Cross-Coupling
abstract: Integrating photochemical catalyst activation and stereochemical control within a single catalyst architecture offers an attractive strategy for asymmetric synthesis. Herein, we report a chiral photoactive nickel catalyst that enables enantioconvergent light-mediated C(sp 2 )–C(sp 3 ) crosscoupling of an N-Boc-protected pyrrolidine-derived trifluoroborate with (hetero)aryl bromides.

title: Soft-drug design for topical JAK1/TYK2 inhibition in atopic dermatitis
abstract: Topical Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors reduce systemic exposure compared with oral dosing, but they do not eliminate it. Ruxolitinib cream, the current topical benchmark in atopic dermatitis (AD), achieves an Eczema Area and Severity Index 75% improvement (EASI-75) rate of 70.0% at week 8 in TRuE-AD4 and itch relief within 15 minutes, yet its plasma concentrations must still be interpreted against a 281 nM threshold linked in vitro to JAK-mediated myelosuppression.

title: Orchestrating literature landscaping in drug discovery by coupling citation expansion with large language models
abstract: Systematic literature reviews guide decisions in drug discovery, yet keyword-based retrieval misses relevant work hidden behind synonyms, compound codes and cross-disciplinary vocabulary. Manual screening of large literature pools is slow and costly. Large language models (LLMs) could relieve this bottleneck, but existing tools address either citation-based retrieval or LLM screening, and rarely validate how well the combination performs.

title: Support Effects in the Catalytic Transfer Hydrogenolysis of Diphenyl Ether over Ru Catalysts
abstract: The selective cleavage of aryl C–O bonds while avoiding hydrogenation of the aromatic ring is a crucial challenge in the reductive valorisation of lignin. Industrial Ru (5 wt%) catalysts supported on wood-derived activated carbon (RuCw) and δ/θ-Al 2 O 3 (RuAl), prepared by deposition–precipitation using Ru recovered from metal-containing waste streams, were compared in diphenyl ether (DPE) hydrogenolysis under catalytic transfer hydrogenolysis (CTH) with 2-propanol and under molecular H 2 .

title: Analytical nuclear gradients for the CC2 method using pair-natural orbitals based on localized virtual molecular orbitals for excited states
abstract: Analytical nuclear energy gradients are indispensable for optimizing excited-state structures and exploring excited-state potential energy surfaces. Local correlation methods based on pair-natural orbitals (PNOs) have extended correlated wavefunction calculations to large molecules, and their analytical gradients have been developed for ground states but, to our knowledge, not for excited states.
